content: The report includes data from 23 external support agencies, which collectively account for over 90% of official development assistance allocated to sanitation and drinking water. It provides national, regional, and global estimates of progress in drinking water, sanitation, and hygiene, using service ladders to benchmark and compare progress across countries at varying stages of development. It aims to encourage healthcare professionals to take individual and collective action to protect children’s health from air pollution. Neonatal care and the prevention and treatment of severe morbidity in young children are critical for optimal child development. The publication Survive and Thrive: Transforming Care for Every Small and Sick Newborn emphasizes the importance of nurses partnering with families to teach caregivers how to meet infants' developmental needs. This includes skin-to-skin contact, breastfeeding, routine caregiving, and sensory stimulation through touch, talking, singing, and gentle motion. Engaging primary caregivers in newborn care strengthens caregiver-newborn bonding and enhances caregiving skills, facilitating a smoother transition to home care. Guidance is also provided for managing serious bacterial infections in young infants when referral to higher-level care is not feasible. This document outlines strategies for resource-limited settings, emphasizing the role of community health workers and home visits in identifying signs of serious infections in neonates and young infants. The Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) framework offers comprehensive materials, including treatment algorithms for conditions such as respiratory infections, diarrhea, fever, malnutrition, anemia, HIV, and well-child care. Both in-person and distance learning modules are available to support healthcare workers. The WHO's Essential Newborn Care Course equips health workers with the skills and knowledge to provide appropriate care during the critical newborn period. It incorporates evidence-based practices from the WHO's guidelines on pregnancy, childbirth, postpartum, and newborn care. A training course for community health workers, developed by WHO and UNICEF, focuses on reducing newborn and child mortality and promoting healthy growth and development. The course includes modules on caring for newborns at home, managing sick children, and supporting healthy growth and development. Home-based maternal, newborn, and child health records serve as a bridge between healthcare providers and families. These records have been shown to improve care-seeking behaviors, male involvement in household support, maternal and child home care practices, infant feeding, and communication between health providers and families. Standards for improving the quality of care for children and adolescents in health facilities emphasize addressing their unique physical, psychosocial, developmental, and communication needs. The framework includes eight domains for improving care quality and focuses on the most common conditions affecting children and adolescents. Guidelines on physical activity, sedentary behavior, and sleep for young children under five years of age are part of the Ending Childhood Obesity initiative. These recommendations aim to promote early childhood development by addressing physical activity levels, reducing screen time, and ensuring adequate sleep. The WHO's implementation plan for ending childhood obesity provides policymakers with a summary of recommended actions. It outlines integrated interventions tailored to specific settings to halt the rise in childhood obesity, recognizing the variability in prevalence, risk factors, and socioeconomic conditions across countries. The effectiveness of caregiving interventions in promoting early learning and socioemotional development during the first three years of life is a key focus. Integrated caregiving and nutrition interventions are also evaluated for their impact on early childhood development and growth outcomes. These interventions address cognitive, motor, and socioemotional development, as well as physical growth indicators such as height-for-age and weight-for-age. The role of maternal mental health in influencing early childhood development outcomes is highlighted. Psychological interventions for depression and anxiety in pregnant and postpartum women are shown to improve child outcomes, including cognitive and motor development, language skills, and emotional well-being. The WHO guidelines emphasize the importance of evidence-based caregiving interventions to support early childhood development. These interventions include parent-child interaction, communication skills, nutrition, caregiver coping strategies, and social support. The guidelines also address the need for high-quality research to inform policy and practice, particularly in lowand middle-income countries.
